item.title: Why Small Tasks Matter
item.description:
Posted on September 4, 2026

Small tasks are the atoms of a productive day. Reply to one message. Put the mug in the dishwasher before it becomes a permanent piece of archaeology.

A todo app gives these tasks a place to land. That matters because the brain is excellent at inventing concerns and less excellent at remembering which one it invented while you were brushing your teeth.

The goal is not to fill every minute. It is to make the next useful action visible, then get on with life.
item.dc:creator: Stijn Ruts

item.title: The Empty List
item.description:
Posted on September 3, 2026

There is a special calm that arrives when the last todo disappears. For a few seconds, the system is stable. Nothing is overdue. No task is silently judging you from a browser tab.

Then someone remembers the groceries.

This is not failure of the system. An empty list is a temporary victory condition, not a permanent lifestyle. The point of a todo app is to make room for the next thing without pretending there will never be another thing.
item.dc:creator: Stijn Ruts

item.title: The Emotional Lifecycle of a Todo
item.description:
Posted on September 2, 2026

Every todo begins as a confident promise: I will do this today.

By lunch, it has become a negotiation: I will do this today, unless today contains unexpected emails. By evening, it is a historical artefact with a surprisingly strong claim to tomorrow.

Completion is the happy ending. Deletion is also acceptable. The mature todo manager understands that not every task needs closure; some need the dignity of being quietly removed after three weeks of avoidance.
item.dc:creator: Stijn Ruts

item.title: The Ancient Art of the Todo List
item.description:
Posted on September 1, 2026

The todo list is older than the smartphone, the startup, and probably even the standing desk. Roman generals had plans. Monks had schedules. Your ancestors had a scrap of papyrus reminding them to buy olives.

The modern todo app is the same idea with better typography and fewer chances of losing the list in a sandal. Its greatest feature is not intelligence. It is the gentle external pressure of seeing a list of unfinished tasks stare back at you.

There is something reassuring about a list that asks for no quarterly review. It only asks: what is the next small thing?
